posts.title: Advanced AI: Agents, RAG, and the Future of Intelligence
posts.subtitle: Is an LLM a brain in a jar? To make it truly useful, we need to give it access to the world. This guide explains RAG and Agents.
posts.brief: Large Language Models are brilliant "brains in a jar." Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) hands them a constantly refreshed memory, while AI Agents give them tools to act in the world. Combined, they turn static knowledge into dynamic, goal-directed intelligence — the next frontier of practical AI.

posts.title: ANN Index Types Explained: When to Choose Flat, HNSW, IVF, or IVF-PQ
posts.subtitle: A production-first guide to picking the right vector index for recall, latency, memory, and update patterns.
posts.brief: If your dataset is small and correctness is critical, use Flat. If you need high recall with low latency and enough RAM, use HNSW. If your corpus is huge and memory is your bottleneck, use IVF-PQ. Start with HNSW for most RAG systems, then move to IVF or IVF-PQ when scale and cost force compression.

posts.title: Big Data 101: The 5 Vs, Ecosystem, and Why Scale Breaks Everything
posts.subtitle: Why traditional databases fail at scale, what the 5 Vs really mean, and a practical map of the big data ecosystem from ingestion to insights.
posts.brief: Traditional databases fail at big data scale for three concrete reasons — storage saturation, compute bottleneck, and write-lock contention. The 5 Vs (Volume, Velocity, Variety, Veracity, Value) frame what makes data "big." A layered ecosystem — Kafka for ingestion, S3 for storage, Spark for processing, Snowflake for serving — assigns one tool per failure mode.

posts.title: The Role of Data in Precise Capacity Estimations for System Design
posts.subtitle: Don't guess. Calculate. We explain how to estimate QPS, Storage, and Bandwidth for your system de...
posts.brief: Capacity estimation is the skill of back-of-the-envelope math that tells you whether your system design will survive its traffic before you write a line of code. Four numbers do most of the work: **DAU, QPS, Storage/day, and Bandwidth/day**.

posts.title: Choosing the Right Database: CAP Theorem and Practical Use Cases
posts.subtitle: Beyond the SQL vs NoSQL debate: A framework for matching database architecture to business requirements.
posts.brief: Database selection is a trade-off between consistency, availability, and scalability. By using the CAP Theorem as a compass and matching your data access patterns to the right storage engine (Relational, Document, KV, or Wide-Column), you can build systems that scale without collapsing under architectural debt.

posts.title: The Consistency Continuum: From Read-Your-Own-Writes to Leaderless Replication
posts.subtitle: Beyond 'Strong vs Eventual': Navigating the subtle trade-offs of distributed agreement.
posts.brief: In distributed systems, consistency is a spectrum of trade-offs between latency, availability, and correctness. By leveraging session-based patterns like Read-Your-Own-Writes and formal Quorum logic ($W+R > N$), architects can provide the illusion of strong consistency while maintaining the horizontal scale of eventual consistency.

posts.title: Azure Cosmos DB API Modes Explained: NoSQL, MongoDB, Cassandra, PostgreSQL, Gremlin, and Table
posts.subtitle: What each API can and cannot do — and the compatibility gaps that break production migrations
posts.brief: Cosmos DB's six API modes are wire-protocol compatibility layers over one shared ARS storage engine — except PostgreSQL (Citus), which is genuinely different. Every API emulates its native database incompletely, and those gaps are structural, not bugs. API mode is permanent and cannot be changed after account creation. NoSQL API is the only one with full Cosmos DB feature access. MongoDB API fails silently on complex aggregation pipelines. Cassandra API lacks materialized views and cross-partition transactions. PostgreSQL API is a managed Citus cluster — a different product entirely. Choose the right API before writing the first byte.

posts.title: Context Window Management: Strategies for Long Documents and Extended Conversations
posts.subtitle: Sliding windows, summarization, RAG, map-reduce, and selective memory strategies for production LLMs
posts.brief: 🧠 Context windows are LLM memory limits. When conversations grow past 4K-128K tokens, you need strategies: sliding windows (cheap, lossy), summarization (balanced), RAG (selective), map-reduce (scalable), or selective memory (precise). LangChain provides `ConversationSummaryMemory` and `ConversationTokenBufferMemory` for production use.

posts.title: Data Warehouse vs Data Lake vs Data Lakehouse: Which One to Choose?
posts.subtitle: Snowflake, Databricks, or S3? We explain the evolution of data storage. Learn when to use a struc...
posts.brief: **Warehouse** = structured, clean data for BI and SQL dashboards (Snowflake, BigQuery). **Lake** = raw, messy data for ML and data science (S3, HDFS). **Lakehouse** = open table formats (Delta Lake, Iceberg) that bring SQL performance to raw storage — the best of both.

posts.title: Elasticsearch vs Time-Series DB: Key Differences Explained
posts.subtitle: Should you store logs in Elasticsearch or InfluxDB? We compare Search Engines vs. Time-Series DBs
posts.brief: Elasticsearch is built for **search** — full-text log queries, fuzzy matching, and relevance ranking via an inverted index. InfluxDB and Prometheus are built for **metrics** — numeric time series with aggressive compression. Picking the wrong one wastes 10× the storage or makes queries 100× slower.

posts.title: HyperLogLog Explained: Counting Billions of Unique Items with 12 KB
posts.subtitle: How stochastic averaging over leading-zero bit runs estimates cardinality to ±0.81% using 12 KB of memory regardless of dataset size.
posts.brief: HyperLogLog estimates the number of distinct elements in a dataset using ~12 KB of memory regardless of cardinality — with ±0.81% error. The insight: if you hash every element to a random bit string, the maximum length of leading zeros you observe is statistically correlated with how many distinct hashes you have seen. Multiple registers stochastically average this observation to reduce variance. Redis ships HyperLogLog as a native data type via `PFADD` and `PFCOUNT`. A HashSet of 100 million unique IDs requires ~800 MB; HyperLogLog requires 12 KB — a 66,000× reduction.

posts.title: ID Generation Strategies in System Design: Base62, UUID, Snowflake, and Beyond
posts.subtitle: How to choose the right uniqueness strategy — from 6-char short URLs to distributed int64 order IDs
posts.brief: Short shareable IDs need Base62 (URL shorteners). Database primary keys at scale need time-ordered IDs (Snowflake, UUID v7). Security tokens need random IDs (UUID v4, NanoID). Picking the wrong strategy either causes B-tree fragmentation at 50M+ rows, production collisions, or IDs that leak your business metrics to competitors.

posts.title: Little's Law: The Secret Formula for System Performance
posts.subtitle: Why does your system slow down when more users join? Little's Law explains the relationship between concurrency, throughput, and latency.
posts.brief: Little's Law ($L = \\lambda W$) connects three metrics every system designer measures: $L$ = concurrent requests in flight, $\\lambda$ = throughput (RPS), $W$ = average response time. If latency spikes, your concurrency requirement explodes with it.

posts.title: LLM Evaluation Frameworks: How to Measure Model Quality (RAGAS, DeepEval, TruLens)
posts.subtitle: Build quality gates for RAG pipelines with RAGAS, DeepEval, and TruLens evaluation frameworks
posts.brief: 📏 Traditional ML metrics (accuracy, F1) fail for LLMs because there's no single "correct" answer. RAGAS measures RAG pipeline quality with faithfulness, answer relevance, and context precision. DeepEval provides unit-test-style LLM evaluation. TruLens enables continuous monitoring in production. The secret: reference-free evaluation using LLMs to judge LLMs.

posts.title: LLM Hallucinations: Causes, Detection, and Mitigation Strategies
posts.subtitle: Why LLMs confidently make things up, how to detect it, and the practical strategies engineers use to keep production AI grounded
posts.brief:
LLMs hallucinate because they are trained to predict the next plausible token — not the next true token. Understanding the three hallucination types (factual, faithfulness, open-domain) plus the five root causes lets you choose the right mitigation: RAG for knowledge gaps, consistency sampling for detection, system-prompt grounding for faithfulness, and NLI-based pipelines for automated verification.

posts.title: LLM Terms You Should Know: A Helpful Glossary
posts.subtitle: A dictionary for the language of Large Language Models. This guide decodes the essential jargon, from Attention to Zero-Shot.
posts.brief: The world of LLMs has its own dense vocabulary. This post is your decoder ring — covering foundation terms (tokens, context window), generation settings (temperature, top-p), safety concepts (hallucination, grounding), and architecture terms (attention, fine-tuning, RAG).

posts.title: Modern Table Formats: Delta Lake vs Apache Iceberg vs Apache Hudi
posts.subtitle: Parquet alone breaks at scale: Delta Lake, Iceberg, and Hudi bring ACID, time travel, and schema evolution to object storage.
posts.brief: Delta Lake, Apache Iceberg, and Apache Hudi are open table formats that wrap Parquet files with a transaction log (or snapshot tree) to deliver ACID guarantees, time travel, schema evolution, and efficient upserts on object storage. Choose Delta Lake for Databricks/Spark-centric shops, Iceberg for multi-engine portability at petabyte scale, and Hudi for near-real-time CDC upserts and streaming pipelines.

posts.title: PagedAttention & KV-Cache Optimization: How vLLM Handles Large Scale Inference
posts.subtitle: How virtual memory paged block mapping solves GPU memory bottleneck and fragmentation in LLM inference.
posts.brief: Large Language Model (LLM) serving is heavily bound by GPU memory capacity due to the Key-Value (KV) cache. Traditional serving frameworks allocate contiguous memory based on maximum sequence length, leading to severe fragmentation and wasted space. This guide explores how PagedAttention, inspired by operating system virtual memory, partitions the KV cache into small logical blocks to enable dynamic, non-contiguous allocations, prefix sharing, and massive throughput gains.

posts.title: PEFT, LoRA, and QLoRA: A Practical Guide to Efficient LLM Fine-Tuning
posts.subtitle: PEFT, LoRA, and QLoRA cut fine-tuning cost while keeping strong task performance.
posts.brief: Full fine-tuning updates every model weight, which is expensive in memory, compute, and storage. PEFT methods update only a small trainable slice. LoRA learns low-rank adapters on top of frozen base weights. QLoRA pushes efficiency further by quantizing base weights (typically 4-bit) while training adapters in higher precision. The right choice depends on your hardware budget, quality target, and deployment constraints.

posts.title: Saga Pattern: Coordinating Distributed Transactions with Compensation
posts.subtitle: Model long-running workflows with compensating actions instead of fragile global transactions.
posts.brief: A Saga replaces fragile distributed 2PC with a sequence of local transactions, each backed by an explicit compensating transaction. Use orchestration when workflow control needs a single brain; use choreography when services must stay loosely coupled.

posts.title: Caching and Persistence in Spark: Storage Levels and When to Use Them
posts.subtitle: Caching in Spark is lazy and partition-level — understanding how StorageLevel and eviction work is the difference between a speedup and an OOM
posts.brief: Calling `cache()` or `persist()` does not immediately store anything — Spark caches lazily at the first action, partition by partition, managed by a per-executor BlockManager. When memory fills up, LRU eviction silently drops or spills partitions. Choosing the right StorageLevel and knowing when NOT to cache is what separates a genuine 5× speedup from an OOM-driven cluster reboot.

posts.title: Stateful Aggregations in Spark Structured Streaming: mapGroupsWithState
posts.subtitle: mapGroupsWithState gives you a per-key mutable state machine in a streaming pipeline — it is the right tool when windows are not enough
posts.brief: `mapGroupsWithState` gives each streaming key its own mutable state object, persisted in a fault-tolerant state store that checkpoints to object storage on every micro-batch. Where window aggregations assume fixed time boundaries, `mapGroupsWithState` lets you model arbitrary state machines — fraud sessions, IoT device lifecycles, complex event patterns — with full control over state transitions, multi-row output, and per-key timeout semantics. The cost is operational: state can grow unboundedly if not explicitly expired, the RocksDB state store requires careful memory tuning, and checkpoint size grows with both key cardinality and state object size.

posts.title: Split Brain Explained: When Two Nodes Both Think They Are Leader
posts.subtitle: How network partitions create two leaders, why that produces irrecoverable data loss, and the quorum, fencing, and STONITH patterns that prevent it
posts.brief: Split brain happens when a network partition causes two nodes to simultaneously believe they are the leader — each accepting writes the other never sees. Prevent it with quorum consensus (at least ⌊N/2⌋+1 nodes must agree before leadership is granted), fencing tokens (each new leader issues a monotonically increasing token; storage layers reject writes below the current high-water mark), and STONITH (physically power off the old leader before the new one begins). Raft, Zookeeper, and etcd enforce quorum by design. MongoDB with `w=1` and Redis Sentinel with `quorum=1` do not — and production incidents prove it.

posts.title: System Design: Complete Guide to Caching — Patterns, Eviction, and Distributed Strategies
posts.subtitle: Cache-Aside to Refresh-Ahead, LRU to ARC — every caching pattern, eviction policy, and distributed strategy you need for system design
posts.brief: Caching is the single highest-leverage performance tool in distributed systems. This guide covers every read/write pattern (Cache-Aside through Refresh-Ahead), every eviction policy (LRU through ARC), cache invalidation pitfalls, thundering herd mitigations, multi-level topologies, and how Twitter, Netflix, and Facebook run caches at planetary scale. Read once; reference forever.

posts.title: System Design Data Modeling and Schema Evolution: Query-Driven Storage That Survives Change
posts.subtitle: Learn how to choose entities, indexes, and schema evolution strategies that match real query patterns at scale.
posts.brief: In system design interviews, data modeling is where architecture meets reality. A good model starts from query patterns, chooses clear entity boundaries, defines indexes deliberately, and includes a schema evolution path so the system can change without breaking reads and writes.

posts.title: System Design: Designing a Financial Ledger with Double-Entry Constraints
posts.subtitle: How to design a highly consistent, idempotent, and auditable double-entry bookkeeping ledger at scale.
posts.brief: Designing a financial ledger requires strict double-entry compliance, high consistency, and complete auditability. Unlike traditional databases where records are updated in-place, a financial ledger must be append-only to preserve a verifiable transaction history. This guide details how to architect a scalable ledger system using relational storage, idempotency mechanisms, and active-active isolation strategies without sacrificing transactional guarantees.

posts.title: System Design HLD Example: Chat and Messaging Platform
posts.subtitle: A clear HLD for real-time chat with ordering, delivery states, and offline synchronization.
posts.brief: A distributed chat system must balance low-latency delivery with strong per-conversation ordering. The architectural crux is the **WebSocket Gateway** for persistent stateful connections and **Cassandra** for append-heavy message storage partitioned by conversation. By using a **Kafka-driven Fan-out** model and **Redis-based Presence** heartbeats, the system can handle millions of concurrent users while ensuring no message is lost, even across device reconnects and network shifts.

posts.title: System Design HLD Example: File Storage and Sync (Dropbox and Google Drive)
posts.subtitle: Build an HLD for file storage, metadata consistency, and cross-device synchronization.
posts.brief: Cloud sync systems separate immutable blob storage (S3) from atomic metadata operations (PostgreSQL), using chunk-level deduplication to optimize storage costs and delta-sync events to minimize bandwidth.

posts.title: System Design HLD Example: Web Crawler
posts.subtitle: A practical interview-ready HLD for a distributed web crawler handling politeness, deduplication, and scale.
posts.brief: A distributed web crawler must balance global throughput with per-domain politeness. The architectural crux is the **URL Frontier**, which manages priority and rate-limiting across a distributed fetcher pool. By combining **Bloom Filters** for URL deduplication and **SimHash** for content near-duplicate detection, the system can crawl billions of pages while maintaining a minimal storage footprint and respecting the stability of the target websites.

posts.title: Real-Time Communication: WebSockets, SSE, and Long Polling Explained
posts.subtitle: When to use WebSockets vs Server-Sent Events vs Long Polling — with real production examples.
posts.brief: 🔌 WebSockets = bidirectional persistent channel — use for chat, gaming, collaborative editing. SSE = one-way server push over HTTP with built-in reconnect — use for AI streaming, live logs, notifications. Long Polling = held HTTP requests — the pragmatic fallback when WebSockets are blocked. Short Polling = simplest but most wasteful — only for low-frequency, low-traffic scenarios. The decisive question is always: *does the client need to send data back in real time?*

posts.title: System Design Sharding Strategy: Choosing Keys, Avoiding Hot Spots, and Resharding Safely
posts.subtitle: A practical guide to shard keys, routing, hot partitions, and how to scale storage without breaking queries.
posts.brief: Sharding means splitting one logical dataset across multiple physical databases so no single node carries all the data and traffic. The hard part is not adding more nodes. The hard part is choosing a shard key that keeps data balanced and queries practical.

posts.title: ACID Properties Explained: How SQL Databases Guarantee Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, and Durability
posts.subtitle: From WAL and MVCC to fsync and isolation levels — the internals behind every ACID guarantee in PostgreSQL, MySQL, Oracle, and SQL Server.
posts.brief: ACID is four orthogonal guarantees that every SQL transaction must provide. Atomicity says all-or-nothing: PostgreSQL implements it via WAL rollback; MySQL InnoDB via undo logs. Consistency says constraints always hold: the database rejects any write that violates a `CHECK`, `FOREIGN KEY`, or `NOT NULL`. Isolation says concurrent transactions cannot see each other's intermediate states: PostgreSQL uses MVCC + Serializable Snapshot Isolation; MySQL InnoDB uses MVCC + Two-Phase Locking. Durability says committed data survives crashes: every major database writes to a write-ahead log and calls `fsync` before acknowledging a commit. Know which property protects which failure class — and know the configuration knobs that let you trade durability for throughput when the workload permits.

posts.title: ACID Transactions in Distributed Databases: DynamoDB, Cosmos DB, and Spanner Compared
posts.subtitle: How modern NoSQL databases achieve atomicity and isolation without a single machine
posts.brief: ACID transactions in distributed databases are not equal. DynamoDB provides multi-item atomicity scoped to 25 items using two-phase commit with a coordinator item, but only within a single region. Cosmos DB wraps partition-scoped operations inside a stored procedure using a JavaScript continuation model — cross-partition writes get no atomic guarantee. Google Spanner is the only cloud database that delivers true global ACID with external consistency, using TrueTime (GPS + atomic clocks) to assign globally ordered timestamps and a commit-wait delay to guarantee causality across datacenters. MongoDB supports multi-document transactions on replica sets but carries measurable performance overhead and does not prevent write skew under snapshot isolation. The right choice depends on atomicity scope, latency tolerance, and operational cost — not on which database claims to be "ACID-compliant."

posts.title: Adapting to Virtual Threads for Spring Developers
posts.subtitle: Migrate your Spring Boot services from thread-pool exhaustion to JDK 21 virtual threads — the practical Spring developer guide
posts.brief: Platform threads (one OS thread per request) max out at a few hundred concurrent I/O-bound requests. Virtual threads (JDK 21+) allow millions — with zero I/O-blocking cost. Spring Boot 3.2 enables them with a single property. Avoid `synchronized` blocks wrapping I/O (they pin virtual threads to OS threads) and CPU-bound work inside virtual threads. For I/O-heavy Spring services, virtual threads are the most impactful JVM upgrade since Java 8 lambdas.

posts.title: Advanced Graph Algorithms: Dijkstra, Topological Sort, and Disjoint Set Union (DSU)
posts.subtitle: Master shortest paths, dependency resolution, and cycle detection with robust Java solutions.
posts.brief: Graph algorithms are the backbone of networking, scheduling, and connection analysis. This guide explores Dijkstra's pathfinding, Topological Sorting for dependency resolution, and Disjoint Set Union (DSU) for cycle detection, complete with runnable Java code.

posts.title: AI Agents Explained: When LLMs Start Using Tools
posts.subtitle: An LLM can talk, but an AI Agent can *act*. We explain how Agents use the ReAct framework to brow...
posts.brief: A standard LLM is a brain in a jar — it can reason but cannot act. An **AI Agent** connects that brain to tools (web search, code execution, APIs). Instead of just answering a question, an agent executes a loop of Thought → Action → Observation until the goal is reached.

posts.title: AI Architecture Patterns: Routers, Planner-Worker Loops, Memory Layers, and Evaluation Guardrails
posts.subtitle: Production AI needs explicit routing, memory, execution, and evaluation layers rather than one loop.
posts.brief: A single agent loop is enough for a demo, but production AI systems need explicit layers for routing, execution, memory, and evaluation. Those layers determine safety, latency, cost, and traceability far more than model choice alone.

articles.title: Big Data 101: The 5 Vs, Ecosystem, and Why Scale Breaks Everything
articles.brief: Traditional databases fail at big data scale for three concrete reasons — storage saturation, compute bottleneck, and write-lock contention. The 5 Vs (Volume, Velocity, Variety, Veracity, Value) frame what makes data "big." A layered ecosystem — Kafka for ingestion, S3 for storage, Spark for processing, Snowflake for serving — assigns one tool per failure mode.

articles.title: The Role of Data in Precise Capacity Estimations for System Design
articles.brief: Capacity estimation is the skill of back-of-the-envelope math that tells you whether your system design will survive its traffic before you write a line of code. Four numbers do most of the work: **DAU, QPS, Storage/day, and Bandwidth/day**.

articles.title: Choosing the Right Database: CAP Theorem and Practical Use Cases
articles.brief: Database selection is a trade-off between consistency, availability, and scalability. By using the CAP Theorem as a compass and matching your data access patterns to the right storage engine (Relational, Document, KV, or Wide-Column), you can build systems that scale without collapsing under architectural debt.

articles.title: The Consistency Continuum: From Read-Your-Own-Writes to Leaderless Replication
articles.brief: In distributed systems, consistency is a spectrum of trade-offs between latency, availability, and correctness. By leveraging session-based patterns like Read-Your-Own-Writes and formal Quorum logic ($W+R > N$), architects can provide the illusion of strong consistency while maintaining the horizontal scale of eventual consistency.

articles.title: Azure Cosmos DB API Modes Explained: NoSQL, MongoDB, Cassandra, PostgreSQL, Gremlin, and Table
articles.brief: Cosmos DB's six API modes are wire-protocol compatibility layers over one shared ARS storage engine — except PostgreSQL (Citus), which is genuinely different. Every API emulates its native database incompletely, and those gaps are structural, not bugs. API mode is permanent and cannot be changed after account creation. NoSQL API is the only one with full Cosmos DB feature access. MongoDB API fails silently on complex aggregation pipelines. Cassandra API lacks materialized views and cross-partition transactions. PostgreSQL API is a managed Citus cluster — a different product entirely. Choose the right API before writing the first byte.

articles.title: Context Window Management: Strategies for Long Documents and Extended Conversations
articles.brief: 🧠 Context windows are LLM memory limits. When conversations grow past 4K-128K tokens, you need strategies: sliding windows (cheap, lossy), summarization (balanced), RAG (selective), map-reduce (scalable), or selective memory (precise). LangChain provides `ConversationSummaryMemory` and `ConversationTokenBufferMemory` for production use.

articles.title: Data Warehouse vs Data Lake vs Data Lakehouse: Which One to Choose?
articles.brief: **Warehouse** = structured, clean data for BI and SQL dashboards (Snowflake, BigQuery). **Lake** = raw, messy data for ML and data science (S3, HDFS). **Lakehouse** = open table formats (Delta Lake, Iceberg) that bring SQL performance to raw storage — the best of both.
articles.primaryConcept: Data Warehouse vs Data Lake vs Data Lakehouse

articles.title: Elasticsearch vs Time-Series DB: Key Differences Explained
articles.brief: Elasticsearch is built for **search** — full-text log queries, fuzzy matching, and relevance ranking via an inverted index. InfluxDB and Prometheus are built for **metrics** — numeric time series with aggressive compression. Picking the wrong one wastes 10× the storage or makes queries 100× slower.

articles.title: HyperLogLog Explained: Counting Billions of Unique Items with 12 KB
articles.brief: HyperLogLog estimates the number of distinct elements in a dataset using ~12 KB of memory regardless of cardinality — with ±0.81% error. The insight: if you hash every element to a random bit string, the maximum length of leading zeros you observe is statistically correlated with how many distinct hashes you have seen. Multiple registers stochastically average this observation to reduce variance. Redis ships HyperLogLog as a native data type via `PFADD` and `PFCOUNT`. A HashSet of 100 million unique IDs requires ~800 MB; HyperLogLog requires 12 KB — a 66,000× reduction.

articles.title: ID Generation Strategies in System Design: Base62, UUID, Snowflake, and Beyond
articles.brief: Short shareable IDs need Base62 (URL shorteners). Database primary keys at scale need time-ordered IDs (Snowflake, UUID v7). Security tokens need random IDs (UUID v4, NanoID). Picking the wrong strategy either causes B-tree fragmentation at 50M+ rows, production collisions, or IDs that leak your business metrics to competitors.
articles.primaryConcept: ID Generation Strategies in System Design

articles.title: Little's Law: The Secret Formula for System Performance
articles.brief: Little's Law ($L = \\lambda W$) connects three metrics every system designer measures: $L$ = concurrent requests in flight, $\\lambda$ = throughput (RPS), $W$ = average response time. If latency spikes, your concurrency requirement explodes with it.

articles.title: LLM Terms You Should Know: A Helpful Glossary
articles.brief: The world of LLMs has its own dense vocabulary. This post is your decoder ring — covering foundation terms (tokens, context window), generation settings (temperature, top-p), safety concepts (hallucination, grounding), and architecture terms (attention, fine-tuning, RAG).

articles.title: Modern Table Formats: Delta Lake vs Apache Iceberg vs Apache Hudi
articles.brief: Delta Lake, Apache Iceberg, and Apache Hudi are open table formats that wrap Parquet files with a transaction log (or snapshot tree) to deliver ACID guarantees, time travel, schema evolution, and efficient upserts on object storage. Choose Delta Lake for Databricks/Spark-centric shops, Iceberg for multi-engine portability at petabyte scale, and Hudi for near-real-time CDC upserts and streaming pipelines.

articles.title: PagedAttention & KV-Cache Optimization: How vLLM Handles Large Scale Inference
articles.brief: Large Language Model (LLM) serving is heavily bound by GPU memory capacity due to the Key-Value (KV) cache. Traditional serving frameworks allocate contiguous memory based on maximum sequence length, leading to severe fragmentation and wasted space. This guide explores how PagedAttention, inspired by operating system virtual memory, partitions the KV cache into small logical blocks to enable dynamic, non-contiguous allocations, prefix sharing, and massive throughput gains.

articles.title: PEFT, LoRA, and QLoRA: A Practical Guide to Efficient LLM Fine-Tuning
articles.brief: Full fine-tuning updates every model weight, which is expensive in memory, compute, and storage. PEFT methods update only a small trainable slice. LoRA learns low-rank adapters on top of frozen base weights. QLoRA pushes efficiency further by quantizing base weights (typically 4-bit) while training adapters in higher precision. The right choice depends on your hardware budget, quality target, and deployment constraints.

articles.title: Saga Pattern: Coordinating Distributed Transactions with Compensation
articles.brief: A Saga replaces fragile distributed 2PC with a sequence of local transactions, each backed by an explicit compensating transaction. Use orchestration when workflow control needs a single brain; use choreography when services must stay loosely coupled.

articles.title: Stateful Aggregations in Spark Structured Streaming: mapGroupsWithState
articles.brief: `mapGroupsWithState` gives each streaming key its own mutable state object, persisted in a fault-tolerant state store that checkpoints to object storage on every micro-batch. Where window aggregations assume fixed time boundaries, `mapGroupsWithState` lets you model arbitrary state machines — fraud sessions, IoT device lifecycles, complex event patterns — with full control over state transitions, multi-row output, and per-key timeout semantics. The cost is operational: state can grow unboundedly if not explicitly expired, the RocksDB state store requires careful memory tuning, and checkpoint size grows with both key cardinality and state object size.

articles.title: Split Brain Explained: When Two Nodes Both Think They Are Leader
articles.brief: Split brain happens when a network partition causes two nodes to simultaneously believe they are the leader — each accepting writes the other never sees. Prevent it with quorum consensus (at least ⌊N/2⌋+1 nodes must agree before leadership is granted), fencing tokens (each new leader issues a monotonically increasing token; storage layers reject writes below the current high-water mark), and STONITH (physically power off the old leader before the new one begins). Raft, Zookeeper, and etcd enforce quorum by design. MongoDB with `w=1` and Redis Sentinel with `quorum=1` do not — and production incidents prove it.

articles.title: System Design: Complete Guide to Caching — Patterns, Eviction, and Distributed Strategies
articles.brief: Caching is the single highest-leverage performance tool in distributed systems. This guide covers every read/write pattern (Cache-Aside through Refresh-Ahead), every eviction policy (LRU through ARC), cache invalidation pitfalls, thundering herd mitigations, multi-level topologies, and how Twitter, Netflix, and Facebook run caches at planetary scale. Read once; reference forever.

articles.title: System Design: Designing a Financial Ledger with Double-Entry Constraints
articles.brief: Designing a financial ledger requires strict double-entry compliance, high consistency, and complete auditability. Unlike traditional databases where records are updated in-place, a financial ledger must be append-only to preserve a verifiable transaction history. This guide details how to architect a scalable ledger system using relational storage, idempotency mechanisms, and active-active isolation strategies without sacrificing transactional guarantees.

articles.title: System Design HLD Example: Chat and Messaging Platform
articles.brief: A distributed chat system must balance low-latency delivery with strong per-conversation ordering. The architectural crux is the **WebSocket Gateway** for persistent stateful connections and **Cassandra** for append-heavy message storage partitioned by conversation. By using a **Kafka-driven Fan-out** model and **Redis-based Presence** heartbeats, the system can handle millions of concurrent users while ensuring no message is lost, even across device reconnects and network shifts.

articles.title: System Design HLD Example: Web Crawler
articles.brief: A distributed web crawler must balance global throughput with per-domain politeness. The architectural crux is the **URL Frontier**, which manages priority and rate-limiting across a distributed fetcher pool. By combining **Bloom Filters** for URL deduplication and **SimHash** for content near-duplicate detection, the system can crawl billions of pages while maintaining a minimal storage footprint and respecting the stability of the target websites.

articles.title: Real-Time Communication: WebSockets, SSE, and Long Polling Explained
articles.brief: 🔌 WebSockets = bidirectional persistent channel — use for chat, gaming, collaborative editing. SSE = one-way server push over HTTP with built-in reconnect — use for AI streaming, live logs, notifications. Long Polling = held HTTP requests — the pragmatic fallback when WebSockets are blocked. Short Polling = simplest but most wasteful — only for low-frequency, low-traffic scenarios. The decisive question is always: *does the client need to send data back in real time?*

articles.title: System Design Sharding Strategy: Choosing Keys, Avoiding Hot Spots, and Resharding Safely
articles.brief: Sharding means splitting one logical dataset across multiple physical databases so no single node carries all the data and traffic. The hard part is not adding more nodes. The hard part is choosing a shard key that keeps data balanced and queries practical.

articles.title: Semantic Tool Retrieval: Scaling Agentic Workflows with Large Toolsets
articles.brief: As AI agents gain more capabilities, managing and selecting from an ever-growing array of tools becomes a critical challenge. This article explores Semantic Tool Retrieval, a pattern that leverages embeddings and vector databases to help agents dynamically discover and utilize the most relevant tools for any given task.
